title: Segregation in Florida and violence against musicians
summary: He tells of Florida in the Ella period, where Buddy Rich was beaten for listening to Lucky Millinder and the Whispering Band of Gold was beaten by police.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: From what I hear. Not until, you know, the late '30s and before the war -- that it started changing somewhat. You know, even then you'd go down 52nd Street, you know. You could play, but you don't mix with the people or --

Well, in fact, in Florida you couldn't even play for a white dance in Florida. I remember when I was there with Ella, when I went to Florida, Chauncey Horton drew $50.00, he sent home and went down to the telegraph station. I get a call to come down there and rescue him because he had too much money. And they wanted to know where this guy got $50.00 at.

And I had to go and get him. He had sent money home to his wife, you know. And it was rough. In fact, they beat Buddy Rich up down there for trying to come and hear -- trying to hear Lucky Millinder's band. Lucky played there in the colored section.
Who was Buddy Rich with at the time?
I don't -- maybe the Tommy -- maybe the Dorsey Brothers, Tommy Dorsey probably.
And the police beat him up, huh?

Yeah. You remember the story of the Whispering Band of Gold? Well, that was a band out of Chicago. They went to Florida. This was in the '20s. And they -- some rich man hired them to play for a party, and some of the guys, the cops caught them and beat them up and beat the guy up that was giving the party.
And some of the guys were crippled for the rest of their life and some of them died from it, and broke up all their instruments. And it was quite a story.
The Whispering Band of Gold. Never heard of them.
